title: The Hidden Oasis
summary: Two siblings follow their grandfather's old clues to find a hidden desert spring, then must decide how to share their discovery responsibly with their village.
poll: Faisal and Noura should have told all their friends about the oasis right away.

versions.title: A Hidden Spring in the Sand
versions.text:
Faisal and Noura live in the desert. Grandpa lives there too. He is old and wise.

Grandpa tells a good story. Long ago, he found a hidden spot. It had cool water. Green trees grew there too. He calls it the oasis.

One hot day, the kids want to find it. Grandpa gives them clues. Look for a big red rock. Look for a dry bed. Look for three rocks like palm trees.

The kids walk far. They pass the red rock. They walk by the dry bed. At last, they see three rocks. They climb up and over.

They find it! A hidden spring! Water comes up from the ground. Green plants grow all around. Tall trees give cool shade.

Noura wants to tell all her friends. Faisal stops her. Too many feet could hurt the plants. Loud noise could scare small animals too.

The two kids stop and think. They go to the elders first. The elders hear them. They make a careful plan.

The elders mark a small path. They keep the spring safe. Small groups can come at a time. The camp now has new water. Faisal and Noura feel proud.

Grandfather often told his favorite story. Long ago, as a boy, he had found a hidden spot near the hills. It had a spring with cool water, and green trees grew all around it. He had always called it the oasis.

One hot day, the two children decided to find it for themselves. Grandfather gave them a few useful clues. Look for a tall red rock near the old path. Look for a dry riverbed that winds through the sand. Look for three rocks shaped like palm trees.

The children walked a long way under the hot sun. They passed the tall red rock right where he said it would be. They followed the dry riverbed until it curved. At last, they spotted three rocks standing close together, and carefully they climbed up and over them.

They found it at last, a hidden spring just like the old story! Clear water bubbled up gently from the ground. Green plants and grass grew all around the water, and tall palm trees gave welcome shade.

The two children stopped walking and thought carefully. They decided they wanted to be kind to this rare gift. Instead of rushing home, they walked to speak with the village elders first, and the elders listened closely to every word.

The elders made a careful plan to protect the spring. They marked out one narrow path so visitors would not harm the plants. Only small groups were allowed to visit at any one time. The village now had clean new water to share, and Faisal and Noura both felt proud of their wise, careful choice.

versions.title: The Hidden Oasis
versions.text:
Faisal and Noura resided in a small desert village, and their grandfather resided there too, a man everyone in the village regarded as remarkably wise because he remembered so much about the surrounding landscape and its long, complicated history.

Grandfather cherished recounting one particular story more than any other, narrating it so frequently that the children could recite entire passages themselves without hesitation. Long ago, as a boy, he had wandered unaccompanied into the nearby hills and discovered a hidden location that nobody else in the village knew existed. It contained a natural spring with cool, transparent water, surrounded by vegetation that flourished thickly all around it. He had always referred to it as the oasis, promising that one day he would reveal precisely how to locate it, once his grandchildren were sufficiently mature to appreciate its significance and treat it with genuine, lasting respect.

One particularly hot afternoon, the two children determined that it was finally time to venture out and search for the oasis themselves. Grandfather provided them with a concise list of landmarks to watch for along the journey: an imposing red rock standing near the ancient path, a desiccated riverbed winding through the sand, and three rocks resembling palm trees, positioned close together near the distant hills.

The children traveled a considerable distance beneath the blazing sun, meticulously checking each landmark as they passed it. They located the towering red rock precisely where grandfather had promised, then followed the winding riverbed until it curved sharply toward the left. Eventually, they spotted the three rocks positioned together, and carefully they clambered up and over them, eager to discover whatever lay beyond the rocky barrier.

They discovered it at last, a hidden spring exactly as the old story had promised! Clear water bubbled gently upward from the ground, and verdant plants alongside soft grass flourished all around the shimmering pool, forming a small but thriving ecosystem amid the surrounding arid sand. Towering palm trees leaned overhead, providing cool, welcome shade from the relentless desert heat.

Noura wanted to dash home immediately and inform every single friend about their exhilarating discovery. Faisal halted her and shook his head slowly, already contemplating what consequences might follow from such impulsive excitement. Too many visitors, he explained, could easily trample the delicate vegetation growing near the water, and boisterous crowds could frighten away the timid desert creatures that depended entirely upon this quiet ecosystem to survive year after year.

The two children ceased walking and reflected seriously upon preserving such a remarkable discovery responsibly, rather than behaving selfishly. Instead of rushing home to boast to their friends, they resolved to consult the village elders first and explain everything they had discovered. The elders listened attentively to every detail and commenced discussing a careful, sustainable arrangement for protecting the spring well into the future.

The elders ultimately concluded that genuine stewardship of the spring mattered considerably more than permitting crowds to rush in all at once. They designated one narrow pathway so visitors would not inadvertently damage the nearby vegetation, and they determined that only small, supervised groups could visit at any particular time, preserving the water supply sustainably for many generations to come. Thanks to the wisdom demonstrated by Faisal and Noura, the village finally possessed clean new water to share safely, and grandfather felt profoundly proud that his old childhood story had ultimately found its proper, fitting conclusion.

versions.title: The Hidden Oasis
versions.text:
Faisal and Noura resided in a small desert village alongside their grandfather, a man widely regarded throughout the community as remarkably wise, since he retained an extraordinary memory of the surrounding landscape and its long, complicated history, details that younger generations had largely forgotten.

Grandfather cherished recounting, above all other tales, the story of a hidden location he had discovered decades earlier as an unaccompanied boy wandering through the nearby hills: a natural spring surrounded by flourishing vegetation, which he had always referred to as the oasis, promising repeatedly that his grandchildren would eventually inherit both its location and the responsibility of protecting it.

Spurred by curiosity one scorching afternoon, the two children resolved to locate the oasis themselves, guided only by grandfather's concise description of several distinctive landmarks: an imposing red rock beside the ancient path, a desiccated riverbed winding through the sand, and three rocks resembling palm trees clustered near the distant hills.

Traveling a considerable distance beneath the blazing sun, the children meticulously verified each landmark in sequence, locating the towering red rock precisely where promised before following the riverbed's sharp leftward curve, until at last they encountered the three clustered rocks and clambered eagerly over them.

What awaited them exceeded every expectation drawn from grandfather's descriptions: clear water bubbling gently from the earth, surrounded by verdant plants and soft grass that together formed a surprisingly thriving ecosystem amid the otherwise arid landscape, shaded overhead by towering, protective palm trees.

Noura's immediate impulse was to dash home and broadcast their exhilarating discovery to every friend imaginable, yet Faisal intervened, recognizing instinctively that unrestrained visitors could trample the delicate vegetation and frighten away the timid creatures that depended entirely on this fragile ecosystem for their continued survival.

Rather than succumbing to that impulsive temptation, the siblings chose instead to consult the village elders directly, recognizing that preserving such a remarkable discovery demanded collective wisdom rather than individual boasting, and the elders, upon hearing every detail, began deliberating a sustainable arrangement for protecting the spring.

Ultimately, the elders concluded that genuine stewardship outweighed the temptation of unrestricted access, designating a single narrow pathway, limiting visits to small supervised groups, and thereby preserving the water supply sustainably for generations still to come, a wise resolution that left both grandfather and his resourceful grandchildren profoundly proud of the outcome.

In the weeks that followed, villagers who had long struggled with scarce water found their daily lives transformed, since the carefully managed oasis provided a dependable supply without ever becoming overcrowded or depleted. Grandfather often walked the narrow path himself, quietly satisfied that the secret he had guarded since boyhood had ultimately benefited the entire community, rather than remaining a private memory confined to his own recollections.

keyWords.definition: a green, watery spot in the middle of a dry desert
keyWords.example: The tired travelers rested at the oasis under the palm trees.

keyWords.definition: kept out of sight, so it is hard to find
keyWords.example: My sister kept a hidden box of stickers under her bed.

keyWords.definition: a place where clean water comes up naturally from the ground
keyWords.example: The farmer's sheep drank from a cool spring near the hill.

keyWords.definition: paying close attention so you do not make a mistake or cause harm
keyWords.example: Be careful when you carry the glass of water.

keyWords.definition: feeling happy about something good you did
keyWords.example: I felt proud when I finished my puzzle by myself.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A boy who gets lost in the desert alone and cannot find the way back home
Two children who find a hidden spring and share it wisely with their village
A camel that finds water in the sand and shows the way to the caravan
A grandfather who builds a new village and teaches the children to farm
questions.why: The story follows Faisal and Noura as they find a hidden spring and then choose to tell the elders so the whole village can share it safely.

wrong.A: Faisal is not alone; Noura is with him the whole time.
wrong.C: No camel finds the water in this story.
wrong.D: Grandfather does not build a village in the story.

questions.stem: What clues did grandfather give the children to find the oasis?
options: A red rock, a dry riverbed, and three rocks like palm trees
A blue flag, a cave, and a well that nobody in the village had ever seen before
A camel path and a star map
A broken fence and an old bridge
questions.why: Grandfather told them to look for a tall red rock, a dry riverbed, and three rocks shaped like palm trees.

wrong.B: The story never mentions a flag, a cave, or a well.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a star map.
wrong.D: There is no fence or bridge in the story.

questions.stem: What did the children see at the oasis?
options: Only sand and stone for many miles
A market and shops full of people
A big city with tall towers
Water, green plants, and palm trees
questions.why: In the story, water bubbled up, green plants grew around it, and palm trees gave shade.

wrong.A: The oasis has much more than sand and stone.
wrong.B: There is no market in the story.
wrong.C: The oasis is not a city.

questions.stem: In the story, the word oasis means —
options: a dry place with no water
a kind of rock
a green, watery spot in the desert
a loud desert storm that blows sand across the whole village for days
questions.why: The story describes the oasis as a spot with water, green plants, and palm trees in the middle of the desert.

wrong.A: The oasis has water, so it is not dry.
wrong.B: A rock is not the same as the oasis.
wrong.D: The oasis is not a storm.

questions.stem: What did the children do right after they found the spring?
options: They went straight to the king to tell him about it
They dug a new well beside the spring before dark
They planted new palm trees around the spring in the sand
Noura wanted to tell her friends, but Faisal stopped her
questions.why: Right after finding the spring, Noura wanted to tell everyone, and Faisal stopped her to think first.

wrong.A: There is no king in the story.
wrong.B: The children do not dig a well.
wrong.C: The children do not plant new trees in the story.

questions.stem: Why did Faisal stop Noura from telling all her friends right away?
options: He wanted to keep the spring a secret
He was afraid of the elders
He worried that too many visitors could hurt the plants and animals
He did not believe that Noura had really found a hidden spring
questions.why: Faisal explains that too many feet could trample the plants and scare the shy animals, so he wanted to be careful.

wrong.A: Faisal still wants the village to know, just carefully.
wrong.B: The story does not say Faisal is afraid of the elders.
wrong.D: Faisal saw the spring too, so he believes Noura.

questions.stem: How did Faisal most likely feel when Noura wanted to run and tell everyone?
options: Excited and careless
Angry at Noura
Bored and tired
Worried and thoughtful
questions.why: Faisal stops and shakes his head slowly, thinking about what could go wrong, which shows he feels worried and thoughtful.

wrong.A: Faisal is not careless; he stops to think.
wrong.B: The story does not show Faisal getting angry.
wrong.C: Faisal is thinking hard, not bored.

questions.stem: Why does the story end with the elders making a plan for the spring?
options: To show that keeping water safe takes careful, shared decisions
To show that elders disagree with children about every single choice
To explain how to build a path
To show that the spring was not important
questions.why: The ending shows that protecting the spring for everyone takes careful planning, not just one person's choice.

wrong.B: The elders listen to the children and agree with them.
wrong.C: The story does not teach path-building steps.
wrong.D: The spring is very important to the whole village.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Faisal was right to stop Noura from telling her friends right away? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think Faisal was right to stop Noura. The story shows that too many visitors could hurt the small plants and scare away the shy animals near the spring. Faisal and Noura went to the elders instead, and the elders made a careful plan so small groups could visit safely. Because of this plan, the whole village got clean new water.

keyWords.definition: to travel through a place to discover what is there
keyWords.example: The scouts wanted to explore the cave near the hills.

keyWords.definition: careful and trustworthy about the effects of your actions
keyWords.example: A responsible student returns borrowed books on time.

keyWords.definition: to keep something safe from harm
keyWords.example: Rangers work to protect rare birds in the park.

keyWords.definition: an older, respected person whose advice a community trusts
keyWords.example: The young fisherman asked a village elder for advice.

keyWords.definition: a feature in the land, such as a rock or riverbed, that helps you find your way
keyWords.example: The old clock tower was a landmark the hikers used to find their way home.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A boy named Faisal travels alone across the desert to find oil, and he sells it to the village for a lot of money and becomes rich.
Two children discover a hidden oasis and choose to share it responsibly through the village elders rather than rushing to tell their friends.
Grandfather builds a new path through the village using only rocks, and the children carry the stones for him.
Noura and Faisal decide the oasis should belong to themselves, so they hide it from the elders and their friends.
questions.why: The story centers on the children's discovery and their responsible choice to involve the elders instead of just their friends.

wrong.A: Faisal is not alone, and the story is not about oil.
wrong.C: Grandfather does not build a path in the story.
wrong.D: The children choose to share the spring with the village, not keep it for themselves.

questions.stem: What three landmarks did grandfather describe to help the children find the oasis?
options: A tall red rock, a dry riverbed, and three rocks shaped like palm trees
A broken fence, a well, and a tower that the children had seen earlier that same week
A market, a mosque, and a school
A sand dune, a cave, and a bridge
questions.why: Grandfather lists exactly these three landmarks for the children to watch for along the way.

wrong.B: These landmarks are not mentioned in the story.
wrong.C: These buildings are not part of grandfather's clues.
wrong.D: These are not the landmarks grandfather describes.

questions.stem: What did the children discover growing around the spring?
options: Only sand and stone, with no green plants
Wheat and corn growing in neat rows
Cactus and thorns in the dry sand
Green plants, soft grass, and palm trees
questions.why: The story describes green plants, soft grass, and palm trees surrounding the pool of water.

wrong.A: Plants and grass grow there, not just sand and stone.
wrong.B: The story does not mention wheat or corn.
wrong.C: No cactus or thorns are described at the spring.

questions.stem: In the story, the word landmark means —
options: a kind of animal
a type of water
a feature used to find your way, like a rock or riverbed
a village leader who is chosen by the children instead of by the elders
questions.why: Grandfather's landmarks, such as the red rock and riverbed, are features the children use to find their way.

wrong.A: A landmark is not an animal.
wrong.B: A landmark is not a type of water.
wrong.D: A landmark is not a person.

questions.stem: Why did Faisal stop Noura from running home to tell her friends?
options: He was jealous of her excitement about the water and wanted it for himself
He worried that crowds could damage the plants and frighten the animals
He wanted to find more water first, before they told anyone
He did not want to share the water with anyone, so he kept it secret
questions.why: Faisal explains that too many visitors could trample the delicate plants and scare away the shy animals.

wrong.A: The story gives no sign that Faisal is jealous.
wrong.C: Faisal is not looking for more water; he is thinking about protecting this spring.
wrong.D: Faisal wants to share it, just carefully, through the elders.

questions.stem: Why did the children decide to consult the village elders instead of their friends?
options: They thought the elders would reward them with money for finding the spring
They were afraid of being punished
The elders already knew about the spring
They wanted a responsible, careful plan rather than quick excitement
questions.why: The children stop to think seriously about being responsible, which leads them to the elders instead of bragging to friends.

wrong.A: The story never mentions a reward.
wrong.B: Nothing suggests the children fear punishment.
wrong.C: The elders learn about the spring only when the children tell them.

questions.stem: What does Faisal's choice to stop Noura reveal about his character?
options: He is thoughtful and considers how his actions affect others
He is impulsive and does not think ahead about what might happen
He is selfish and wants the water for himself and his own family
He is afraid of his grandfather and does not want to be scolded
questions.why: Faisal pauses to think about the plants and animals before acting, which shows he considers the effects of his actions.

wrong.B: Faisal is the one who stops to think, unlike an impulsive reaction.
wrong.C: Faisal wants the village to share the water safely, not keep it for himself.
wrong.D: The story gives no sign that Faisal fears his grandfather.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the story?
options: By comparing two different deserts found in separate faraway countries of the world with their deserts
By describing grandfather's entire life story from his childhood until his old age
By following the children from discovering the spring to making a responsible plan with the elders
By listing facts about palm trees without ever mentioning Faisal or Noura
questions.why: The story moves in order from grandfather's clues, to the discovery, to the children's choice, and finally to the elders' plan.

wrong.A: The story does not compare different deserts.
wrong.B: The story focuses on one event, not grandfather's whole life.
wrong.D: The story is not a list of facts about trees.

MID.prompt: Explain why Faisal and Noura chose to tell the village elders instead of rushing to tell their friends. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained the children's reason clearly.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Faisal and Noura chose to tell the village elders because they wanted to be responsible with their discovery. Faisal worried that too many visitors could trample the delicate plants and frighten the shy desert animals near the spring. Instead of rushing home to boast to their friends, the children walked straight to the elders, who listened closely and made a careful, sustainable plan so small groups could visit safely.

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without running out or causing harm
keyWords.example: The farmers switched to a more sustainable way of watering their crops.

keyWords.definition: to keep something safe and unharmed, especially for the future
keyWords.example: The museum works to preserve old maps of the region.

keyWords.definition: to ask someone experienced for advice before deciding something
keyWords.example: Before changing the schedule, the coach decided to consult the team.

keyWords.definition: a community of living things and their surroundings, all connected together
keyWords.example: A single pond can support a surprisingly complex ecosystem.

keyWords.definition: the careful and responsible management of something valuable, especially for others
keyWords.example: Good stewardship of a shared garden means everyone helps care for it.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Two siblings fight constantly over who found the spring first, and they stop speaking to each other and their friends for a whole year.
The story mainly explains how iron oxide colors desert sand, and it follows a scientist who studies red dunes for many years.
A hidden desert spring tests two children's judgment, and their choice to consult the elders turns a personal discovery into a sustainably shared resource.
Grandfather forbids the children from ever mentioning the oasis to anyone, and he sends them away from the village for good, far away across the open sand and the dunes.
questions.why: The story's turning point is the children choosing stewardship and consultation over impulsive excitement, which lets the whole village benefit safely.

wrong.A: The siblings do not fight over the discovery.
wrong.B: The story never discusses iron oxide or sand color.
wrong.D: Grandfather wants them to eventually share it, not hide it forever.

questions.stem: According to the story, what kind of ecosystem formed around the spring?
options: A small but thriving cluster of plants, grass, and palm trees
A market filled with traders selling goods near the edge of the village square
A cave full of bats
A frozen lake
questions.why: The story describes a small but thriving ecosystem of plants, soft grass, and palm trees surrounding the pool.

wrong.B: No market appears at the spring.
wrong.C: The story never mentions bats or a cave.
wrong.D: The spring is a desert pool, not a frozen lake.

questions.stem: What specific role did the village elders play once Faisal and Noura told them about the spring?
options: They ignored the children and told them to go home
They sold the land to outsiders who wanted to build a hotel
They forbade anyone from ever visiting the spring, even the elders themselves
They designed a sustainable plan limiting visits and protecting the plants
questions.why: The elders marked a narrow path, limited visits to small groups, and protected the plants, creating a sustainable arrangement.

wrong.A: The elders listen closely to every detail.
wrong.B: The story never mentions selling the land.
wrong.C: The elders allow small supervised groups to visit, not no one at all.

questions.stem: In the story, stewardship most nearly means —
options: selling a resource for the highest profit
responsible care and management of something valuable
exploring unknown territory without any plan, landmarks, or guidance
a type of desert plant
questions.why: The elders practice stewardship by carefully managing and protecting the spring for the community's long-term benefit.

wrong.A: Stewardship is not about selling anything for profit.
wrong.C: Exploring is what the children do earlier; stewardship is the elders' careful management.
wrong.D: Stewardship is not a plant.

questions.stem: What was the main effect of Faisal's decision to stop Noura from telling her friends?
options: The spring was destroyed by big crowds who came to see it and splash in it
The village lost interest in the spring after about a week or two
The discovery was protected until a careful, sustainable plan could be made
Noura never spoke to Faisal again after that day, and she was sad
questions.why: Because Faisal paused the excitement, the spring stayed undamaged until the elders could design a careful, sustainable plan.

wrong.A: The spring is protected, not destroyed.
wrong.B: The village gains a valuable new water source, showing clear interest.
wrong.D: The story shows no lasting conflict between the siblings.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about grandfather's reason for waiting to reveal the oasis's exact location?
options: He had forgotten exactly where it was after so many years away from those hills
He was never actually sure the oasis existed
He planned to sell the location to visitors
He wanted the children to be mature enough to handle the responsibility wisely
questions.why: Grandfather promises to reveal the location once his grandchildren are mature enough to treat it with respect, showing he valued their readiness.

wrong.A: Grandfather clearly remembers precise landmarks.
wrong.B: Grandfather is confident the oasis exists, since he found it himself.
wrong.C: The story never mentions selling the location.

questions.stem: Which best describes the difference between Faisal's and Noura's immediate reactions to the discovery?
options: Noura's instinct was to celebrate openly, while Faisal immediately weighed the discovery's risks
Faisal wanted to keep the spring secret, while Noura wanted to destroy it with stones
Both children reacted with identical caution, and both wanted to wait before telling anyone
Noura distrusted the elders, while Faisal trusted them and wanted to tell them first
questions.why: Noura's first impulse is to rush and tell every friend, while Faisal immediately considers the consequences of crowds on the fragile ecosystem.

wrong.B: Faisal does not want to hide it forever, and Noura never wants to destroy it.
wrong.C: Their reactions clearly differ, not match.
wrong.D: Both children end up trusting and consulting the elders.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that villagers' daily lives were transformed by the carefully managed oasis?
options: To prove that the oasis was never actually useful
To show the real, lasting benefit of the children's responsible choice
To criticize the village elders for responding far too slowly to the discovery
To suggest that one person should have controlled the water alone
questions.why: This detail shows that the children's responsible decision led to a dependable, sustainable benefit for the whole community, not just excitement in the moment.

wrong.A: The oasis clearly becomes very useful to the village.
wrong.C: The elders act quickly and thoughtfully once told.
wrong.D: The story shows the water is shared carefully among the community, not controlled by one person.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says Faisal and Noura should have told all their friends about the oasis right away. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about responsibility, stewardship, and the elders' plan.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that Faisal and Noura should have told all their friends right away. The story shows that rushing to share the discovery could have led crowds to trample the delicate plants and frighten away the animals that depended on the fragile ecosystem. By consulting the village elders instead, the children made the responsible, sustainable choice: the elders designed a plan with a narrow path and limited small-group visits, which protected the spring and let the whole village benefit safely for years. Someone might argue that friends deserved to know immediately, but the story shows that genuine stewardship sometimes means pausing excitement in favor of a wiser, shared plan.

LOW.stem: What did Grandpa do long ago?
options: He built a camp
He sold some trees
He lost his way home
He found a hidden spot
LOW.why: The text says that long ago he found a hidden spot with cool water.

wrong.A: The text does not say he built a camp.
wrong.B: The text does not say he sold trees.
wrong.C: He found the spot; the text does not say he got lost.

LOW.stem: In the story, the word clues means —
options: hints to find something
water from the ground
plants that grow in sand
kids who walk far
LOW.why: Grandpa gives clues, like the red rock, to help the kids find the oasis.

wrong.B: Water from the ground is the spring.
wrong.C: The clues are rocks and a dry bed.
wrong.D: The kids use the clues; they are not the clues.

LOW.stem: What could too many feet do at the spring?
options: Make the water cold
Hurt the plants
Bring new trees
Dry up the sand
LOW.why: Faisal says too many feet could hurt the plants.

wrong.A: The text does not talk about cold water.
wrong.C: Feet do not bring trees.
wrong.D: The text does not say feet dry up sand.

LOW.stem: What did the kids pass right after the red rock?
options: Three tall trees
A hidden spring
The dry bed
A big camp
LOW.why: The kids passed the red rock and then walked by the dry bed.

wrong.A: The trees are at the spring, at the end.
wrong.B: They find the spring last.
wrong.D: The camp is where the kids started.

MID.stem: How did grandfather first find the oasis?
options: He followed a map he had drawn
He dug a deep well in the sand
He wandered the hills as a boy
He got a clue from the elders
MID.why: The story says that as a boy he wandered into the hills and discovered it.

wrong.A: No map is mentioned.
wrong.B: The spring was already there; he did not dig it.
wrong.D: The elders are not part of his discovery.

MID.stem: In the story, the word trample means to —
options: water the plants well
step on and crush
plant seeds in rows
carry them far away
MID.why: Faisal says too many feet could trample small plants, which means step on and crush them.

wrong.A: Feet do not water plants.
wrong.C: Planting is not what feet do here.
wrong.D: Feet harm the plants; they do not carry them.

MID.stem: Why did the elders mark one narrow path?
options: To keep the plants safe
So the spring would run dry
So the animals could not drink
So the path would be hard to find
MID.why: The story says the path was marked so visitors would not damage the plants nearby.

wrong.B: The elders wanted to protect the spring.
wrong.C: The elders wanted to protect the animals too.
wrong.D: The path was marked to help visitors.

MID.stem: What does "just like the old story had promised" tell us?
options: The story was not really true
Grandfather's story was true
The oasis was very far away
The children made it all up
MID.why: The children find the spring just as grandfather described, so his story was true.

wrong.A: The children found what the story described.
wrong.C: The story gave landmarks; it did not say how far.
wrong.D: The children found a real spring.

HIGH.stem: What did the children do right after following the dry riverbed until it curved?
options: Spoke with the elders
Spotted the three rocks
Found the red rock
Drank the spring water
HIGH.why: They followed the riverbed to its curve, and at last spotted the three rocks.

wrong.A: They saw the elders after the spring.
wrong.C: They found the red rock before the riverbed.
wrong.D: They reached the spring after the rocks.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the word delicate describes plants that are —
options: easy to damage
very tall
bright green
full of water
HIGH.why: Faisal worries visitors could trample the delicate plants, so they are easily damaged.

wrong.B: The plants near the water are small, not tall.
wrong.C: Their color is not what the word describes.
wrong.D: The word describes how easily they break.

HIGH.stem: Why did the elders let only small groups visit at one time?
options: To make the path longer
To keep the water supply lasting
To hide the spring from friends
To save time for the village
HIGH.why: In the story, small groups keep the water supply sustainable for generations.

wrong.A: The path was marked to protect plants.
wrong.C: The elders wanted to share the water safely.
wrong.D: Saving time is not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: What can you infer about grandfather's old story from what the children found?
options: It was true
It was made up
It was about a big city
It was told by Faisal
HIGH.why: The children found the clear spring among trees that grandfather had described, so his story was true.

wrong.B: What they found matched his words, so it was not made up.
wrong.C: The story was about a spring in the desert.
wrong.D: Grandfather told the story, not Faisal.
